\section{Audit of the literature: how often are the controls of the protocol used?}
\label{sec:m-litaudit}

To check whether the controls of the protocol are common practice, 23 papers that propose a learned selector or controller of operators, strategies or parameters inside a metaheuristic for a combinatorial problem were coded, in two rounds: 12 papers in round 1 (eight fixed queries plus four added before reading any paper; protocol and codebook frozen before any paper was read, \texttt{analysis/litaudit\_codebook\_entrada159.md}) and 11 in round 2 (an amendment that changes only the sampling, \texttt{analysis/litaudit\_codebook\_round2\_entrada172.md}, frozen with a hash before any new paper was read: the same codebook, the same source and criteria, new field-qualified queries because the free-text ones returned mostly off-topic papers). The source is arXiv, 2015--2026, open full text; every exclusion (17 in all) is listed with its reason in \texttt{results/litaudit\_entrada159.csv} and \texttt{results/litaudit\_round2\_entrada172.csv}. The second round stopped at 11 papers, below the target of $18$, because the queries were exhausted. Coding is conservative: ``U'' (cannot be determined from the text) counts as not demonstrated, and a common time limit counts as an equal-CPU budget. The sample is small, restricted to open-access arXiv papers, and coded by one coder (an AI assistant, reading the full text by retrieval with one question per item); eight papers drawn at random from the pooled sample are listed for double coding by the author (2206.03185, 2206.05694, 2304.04022, 2305.02805, 2312.16767, 2408.14864, 2505.23098, 2607.02315; \texttt{results/entrada172\_litaudit.txt}). \todonote{to improve: obtain papers through the institution to reach $30$ or more, and have the eight papers above double-coded by the author}

The cheap controls are fairly common: a random-selection control in 10 of 23 papers and a variant of the same host without the learned policy in 15. The controls that make a comparison budget-fair are rarer: only 6 of 23 compare with the variants without learning at a common time limit (5 at equal iterations or evaluations, 3 mixed, 9 not stated), 3 include a static configuration tuned offline as a competitor, 6 state that tuning or training instances are separate from the test instances, and 2 of the 10 that use a statistical test correct for multiple comparisons. 22 of the 23 papers conclude that the learned component helps (five of them with mixed evidence); the other one claims a different gain, that of parallelism, and none reports a null result for the policy. Predictions recorded before reading: in round 1 five of seven were wrong (random controls, ablations, overhead reports, statistical tests and multiplicity were more common than predicted; equal-CPU comparisons and offline-tuned competitors were rare, as predicted); in round 2, registered for the pooled sample, five of seven held, and the two misses are at the boundary (an equal-time-limit share of $26\%$ against a predicted $<25\%$, and $2$ of $10$ testers correcting for multiplicity against $<20\%$, one of them through Tukey intervals). The pre-fixed reading of the amendment (the budget-fair controls are rare if both the equal-time-limit and the offline-tuned shares are below a third) holds ($26\%$ and $13\%$). The audit therefore supports the rows of Table~\ref{tab:fair_vs_naive} that rest on equal iterations and on the absence of an offline-tuned competitor, and not a claim that random controls are uncommon.
